variants.note: the negative contraction of **shall not**, used mainly in British English
the usual weak form before a verb, as in *I shall go*

core_idea: **Shall** is used, mainly with I and we, to talk about the future in formal English, to make an offer or a suggestion, or, in legal and official writing, to state a rule.

senses.definition: used with I or we, mainly in formal or British English, to talk about what will happen
senses.explanation: In everyday American English, **will** has mostly replaced **shall** for the plain future. **Shall** with **I** or **we** still sounds natural in formal writing and in fairly formal British speech.

examples.text: I shall return by six o'clock.
We shall be in touch once we have more details.
I shan't be able to come after all.

synonyms.note: **will** is the everyday word for the future with any subject

compare.note: **shall** with **I** or **we** is more formal and less common than **will**, which works with every subject

adaptation.grammar: **Shall** is normally used only with **I** or **we**; for other subjects, English uses **will**.

senses.definition: used in a question with I or we to offer to do something or to suggest doing something together
senses.explanation: A common, everyday use in both American and British English, quite different from the formal future use.

examples.text: Shall we go for a walk?
What shall we do this weekend?

senses.definition: used in official rules, laws, and contracts to state what someone is required to do
senses.explanation: A formal use found in legal and official documents, where it has the force of **must**, with any subject, not only **I** or **we**.

examples.text: The tenant shall pay rent on the first of each month.
Members shall attend at least three meetings a year.
This agreement shall remain in effect for one year.

synonyms.note: **must** is the everyday equivalent; **shall** is kept for legal and official style

adaptation.culture: This legal use is found in contracts, laws, and rulebooks; it would sound strange in ordinary conversation, where **must** or **has to** is used instead.

usage_note: American English mostly uses **will** for the plain future with every subject; **shall** with **I** or **we** now sounds formal or old-fashioned there, though it remains natural in fairly formal British speech and writing. **Shall I...?** and **Shall we...?** for offers and suggestions are common and natural in both varieties. In legal and official writing, **shall** states a rule with the force of **must**.

learner_errors.note: The plain future use of **shall** is mainly limited to **I** and **we**; other subjects take **will**.
A modal such as **shall** is followed by the base form of a verb without **to**.

see_also.note: the everyday word for the future with any subject

adaptation.grammar: **Shall** is a modal: it takes the base form of a verb with no **to**, adds no **-s**, and has no infinitive or -ing form of its own.
